blocks.text: Daniel unplugged the collector before Laura reached the bench.
He wound the disconnected cable around the trolley rail and moved the iron tray aside.
Laura had expected another test. She kept her coat on.
“Where are we taking it?”
“Upstairs.”
She looked toward the narrow door at the back of the workshop. Beyond it, a flight of iron steps turned beneath a low ceiling. The trolley would not fit through the door.
Daniel lifted the Army ray from its bench.
Luke drifted out of the way. His uncle waited until both of them were clear, moved the toggle to blue and aimed at the collector. The copper rings on the barrel caught the light.
For a moment, the trolley stood inside a pale shimmer. Then its wheels drew together, its glass shortened and the great brass mouth became a little yellow bell.
Laura stepped closer.
The machine stood scarcely a foot long, its cable wound like black thread around the rail. A trace of orange remained inside the glass.
Daniel slid a piece of board beside it and carefully lifted the trolley onto the wood.
“Take the ray.”
Laura caught both handles when he passed it to her. It was heavier than she expected. She lowered the barrel toward the floor and followed him past the full-size tank.
Luke went ahead to check the stairs.
Daniel edged around the landing, his coat catching on a bolt. Laura freed it while he kept the board level.
At the top, Luke called back that the door was open.
Wind came down the last few steps. Laura pushed through into sunlight.
Daniel carried the little collector out onto the roof as though he were bringing someone a cake.
blocks.alt: Daniel carries the miniaturized collector on a board through the rooftop doorway while Laura carries the separate Army ray and bodyless Luke checks ahead.

blocks.text: The stairhouse stood against the western wall of the lower annex. The adjoining warehouse rose another two stories above it. Low in the wall, a bricked-up window left a pale rectangle with its sill just above roof level.
The rest of the roof spread eastward, tar and gravel broken by patched seams. A low parapet enclosed the northern edge. Beyond it, chimneys and taller buildings rose toward the center of Cleveland.
Laura could see Terminal Tower between two rooftops.
Daniel paced out a place beside a low metal ventilator.
“There’s a drain on that side,” Luke said.
A shallow gutter led east to an opening beneath the parapet.
“We'll stay above it.”
Daniel set the board on a clear patch of roofing and took the ray from Laura. She and Luke moved behind him.
Daniel shifted the toggle to red.
The little wheels swelled. Copper spread around the lengthening glass. Laura took another step back as the brass funnel rose to its familiar height.
The collector settled with a clatter.
One wheel turned.
Daniel put down the ray and caught the rail. The trolley stopped, then edged forward again when he loosened his grip.
“Hold this.”
Laura crossed to the other side. The wheel beneath her pivoted toward the gutter. She pushed the lower frame, feeling its weight come against her arms.
“Your side,” Luke said. “The wheel's caught sideways.”
Daniel pulled. The caster jumped the raised edge of a tar patch and the whole trolley lurched toward Laura.
Her boots slid through the gravel. She bent her knees and drove her shoulder against the rail, keeping clear of the glass above it.
blocks.alt: Laura braces the restored collector’s lower frame while Daniel steadies the opposite side and Luke guides them past a caught caster on the sloping roof.

blocks.text: “Stop pulling!”
Laura braced the machine while Luke checked the ground.
“There's a flat patch behind you. About a foot.”
“Together,” she told Daniel.
They eased the trolley over the seam onto the flatter patch.
She straightened, rubbing her shoulder.
Daniel fetched two scraps of timber and chocked opposite wheels.
Daniel faced the brass mouth north toward the ventilator, keeping the gap as short as the successful test downstairs.
The vent stood six feet beyond the lip of the funnel. Its squat metal housing was bolted to a concrete base, with enough room on its southern side for someone to sit facing the machine.
The northern parapet lay clear beyond the vent.
The control panel faced west. Between it and the warehouse wall lay an open strip about eight feet wide. Luke could move there without drifting across the intake.
Daniel unwound the cable. It would not reach the stairhouse.
Laura looked at him.
He looked at the short plug in his hand, put it down and went downstairs.
Luke remained beside the meters.

The wind lifted the ends of Laura's ponytail. Below them, someone shut a loading door. She went to the parapet and looked down at the street, where a man was wheeling a stack of cartons toward a truck.
He never looked up.
From here she could watch him without seeing his expression change when he noticed her mask. She stayed until Daniel returned, breathing hard, with a heavy extension cord over one shoulder.

He plugged it into a socket just inside the stairhouse. Laura helped him feed it beneath the door. They ran it close to the warehouse wall, then turned it across the clear strip to the collector's western side.
The cable lay behind their working positions, leaving the intake clear.
blocks.alt: The collector faces the low northern vent, with its western control panel and cable clear of the approach; the taller intact warehouse wall stands beside the rooftop stairhouse.

blocks.text: He switched on the collector.
Luke watched the dials while Daniel worked the switch.
The thin captured glow flickered between the coils. Neither needle climbed.
“Same as downstairs,” Luke said.
Daniel switched it off and wiped a dusty handprint from the glass.
Laura moved to the vent. From there, the funnel looked larger than it had from the parapet. If Flaming Head came down in front of her, he would have his back to it.
She imagined the bright face turning when the hum began.
Daniel carried the ray toward the stairhouse, pausing at the parapet.
Below, trucks and cars waited behind a delivery van. None could move until it did.
Daniel held the ray by its handles and looked down its short copper barrel. Then he looked beyond the traffic, across roofs and taller buildings.
Laura called his name.
He lowered the device.
“What?”
“You wanted him close. He's not going to float into that thing because I ask nicely.”
Daniel set the ray on its board just inside the stairhouse and returned with a coil of rope.
Luke stopped beside the control panel.
Daniel laid the rope on the ventilator.
“He came when you needed help before.”
Laura’s hand tightened on the edge of the metal housing. She remembered the fire above the lake, the voice that had reached her silently inside her mind. She had wanted someone to answer her then.
She looked at the rope.
“You want him to think you've caught me.”
“I want him to come down to you.”
Daniel stepped back toward the parapet, leaving her with the rope.
Laura picked up the loose end. Ordinary rope. She could feel its roughness through the leather of her glove.
Flaming Head had made her the costume and waited patiently through every miss.
Across the roof, Daniel waited. Behind him, the city caught the last strong light of the afternoon.
blocks.alt: Daniel surveys Cleveland while Laura stands beside the rope on the vent and agrees to lure Flaming Head; Luke remains near the collector controls.

blocks.text: Laura set the rope back on the vent.
“All right,” she said. “I'll call him.”
